warmup.q: Two threads each run count++ one million times on a shared int count = 0. What does count hold at the end, most of the time?
options: Less than 2,000,000, and a different number each run
warmup.why: Each count++ is a read, an add and a write. When both threads read the same old value, one of the two increments is lost. How many get lost depends on timing, so the number changes from run to run. Nothing throws, because Java doesn't detect races for you. The first section runs exactly this program.

opening:
Picture a bank. It keeps a balance for each account. When money arrives, its program adds the amount to the balance. On payday, deposits pour in, so the program handles them on eight threads, eight paths of work running at once, like eight tellers at a bank's counter.

The next morning, someone checks the account against the program's log, the file where each thread notes what it did. Every log line says its deposit went through, yet the balance is a few thousand dollars short. The log is telling the truth, and so is the balance. They just don't agree.

The line behind it looks like one step: balanceCents += cents. On one thread it's correct, and it passes every small test.

A thread's life ended with a promise: two threads, one counter, and a wrong answer with no warning. This lesson keeps it, with money in it. We'll make a counter lose updates and look inside count++. Then we'll find the bug's two shapes in the bank, and fix each one. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a bank account that came up short while every log line said yes. We watched count++ lose updates and opened it into a read, an add and a write. Then we found the same shapes in the bank's deposits and in its check for recorded payments. Each fix was one atomic step on one key.

Now search some Java or Kotlin code, your own or an open-source project, for containsKey(. Any hit followed by a put on a map that several threads share is check-then-act, waiting for a busy day.

Next, we'll use synchronized to make a whole transfer one atomic step, and find out what a lock promises, and to whom.

sections.h: The smallest race: two threads add to one counter
sections.html:
Let's shrink the bank down to the smallest program that can go wrong. Two threads share one counter, and each adds one to it a million times. Both versions start the same two threads on the same loop:

Java
static volatile int count = 0;

Runnable work = () -> {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) count++;
};
Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work);
a.start(); b.start();
a.join(); b.join();
System.out.println(count);   // 2,000,000? Let's see.
Kotlin
@Volatile var count = 0

val work = { repeat(1_000_000) { count++ } }
val a = thread { work() }
val b = thread { work() }
a.join(); b.join()
println(count)               // 2,000,000? Let's see.

Two things changed in Kotlin: thread { } creates and starts each thread for us, and @Volatile is an annotation where Java has a keyword. Each version joins both threads before it prints. As A thread's life showed, once join(), which waits for a thread to end, returns, main sees everything that thread wrote, so this prints the counter's real final value.

I'd expect 2,000,000. Here's what RaceDemo, the same program in the labs, printed in five runs on a 4-core Linux machine. (A core is a part of the processor that runs one thread at a time.)

run 1: expected 2,000,000, got 1,282,924 (lost 717,076)
run 2: expected 2,000,000, got 1,288,616 (lost 711,384)
run 3: expected 2,000,000, got 1,324,641 (lost 675,359)
run 4: expected 2,000,000, got 1,513,931 (lost 486,069)
run 5: expected 2,000,000, got 2,000,000 (lost 0)

Four wrong answers and one right one, from the same code. Nothing crashed, and there was no exception, no warning and no log line. The program did its arithmetic wrong, by a different amount each time.

That's a race condition: a bug where the result depends on how the threads happen to take turns. The fifth run deserves a second look. Sometimes the threads don't collide, and then a racy program prints the right answer.

One word in the listing needs explaining. volatile is a keyword that makes every thread see a field's newest value, and it's there only to keep the demo honest. Without it, the JIT compiler may keep count in a register, a tiny storage slot inside the core, for the whole loop, and write it back once at the end. (The JIT compiler is the part of the JVM, the program that runs your Java code, that turns code that runs often into fast machine code.) Then some runs lose almost nothing, which hides the bug without fixing it. And volatile doesn't make count++ safe either: it was on the field for all five runs.

Now shrink the loop to 1,000 increments per thread. All five runs print exactly 2,000. The first thread finishes its thousand before the second has even started, so the two never overlap. A race is shy around small numbers. That's why races pass small tests and then fail on a busy day, when many people use the program at once.

A test whose threads never collide proves nothing about thread safety. Make them collide.

So a line as short as count++ can lose updates. It's short only in Java, though. Let's look at what the JVM actually runs.

try.title: Watch the counter lose updates
steps: Open RaceDemo (or its Kotlin twin) in the labs project. Before you run it, write down the total you expect.
Run it from labs/ with the command below, and note how many updates each run loses.
Now add -Pargs=1000 to the command. Predict first: will a thousand increments per thread lose any?

code.title: RaceDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03; /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ public class RaceDemo { // volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. static volatile int count = 0; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 1_000_000; for (int run = 1; run <= 5; run++) { count = 0; Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < perThread; i++) count++; }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.printf("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)%n", run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count); } } }

alt.title: RaceDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // @Volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. @Volatile private var count = 0 /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val perThread = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 1_000_000 for (run in 1..5) { count = 0 val work = { repeat(perThread) { count++ } } val a = thread { work() } val b = thread { work() } a.join(); b.join() println("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)".format(run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count)) } }

try.expect: With a million per thread, most runs lose hundreds of thousands of updates, a different number each time, and now and then a run comes out right. With 1,000 per thread you'll almost always get exactly 2,000, because each thread finishes before the other gets going. Same bug, no symptom.

sections.h: Inside count++: a read, an add and a write
sections.html:
The total came out short because count++ isn't one step, and the bytecode can prove it. Bytecode is the list of simple instructions that javac, the Java compiler, turns your code into, and it's what the JVM runs. Here is the bytecode for the loop body of RaceDemo, as javap -c -p, a JDK tool that prints bytecode, shows it (trimmed):

getstatic  count   // read the current value of count
iconst_1           // load the number 1
iadd               // add the two
putstatic  count   // write the result back to count

Read it aloud: fetch count, add one, store the result back in count. That's a read, an add and a write (loading the 1 only sets up the add). A thread can be paused between any two of those instructions. On a machine with several cores, another thread can run the same instructions at the same moment.

So let's trace the smallest case: two threads, one increment each, with count at 41.

  1. T1 reads count: 41.
  2. T2 reads count: 41.
  3. T1 adds one and writes 42.
  4. T2 adds one and writes 42.

Two increments ran, and the counter moved by one. That's a lost update. A third thread that comes along later reads 42 and carries on, so nothing later in the program ever learns an increment went missing.

The pattern behind the lost update has a name: read-modify-write. You read a value, compute a new one from it, and write it back, assuming nobody changed it in between. Kotlin's count++ on a var compiles to the same three steps, so it races in exactly the same way.

The cure is to make the read, the add and the write happen as one step that no other thread can split. A step like that is atomic: other threads see it either not started or completely done, never halfway.

In the simulator below, you are the scheduler, the part of the operating system that decides which thread runs next. Try to end two increments with count = 1, then try for 2. Getting 2 means letting each thread finish its whole increment before the other starts, which is what an atomic step guarantees.

To check the bytecode yourself, run the demo once, then run this from labs/ and look inside lambda$main$0:

javap -c -p concurrency/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.class

count++ is a toy, though. The bank runs the same three steps on money, and it keeps its balances in a map that calls itself thread-safe.

sim.title: Two threads run count++
sim.intro: You are the scheduler. Click a thread to run its next line. Can you end with count = 1?

goal.say: Lost update. Both threads read 0 before either wrote, so two increments produced 1.

video.title: Why count++ lies: three steps, two threads, one lost update

sections.h: Lost deposits in the bank, even on a thread-safe map
sections.html:
The bank's deposit is count++ with money in it:

Java
void deposit(long cents) {
    balanceCents += cents;     // read, add, write
}
Kotlin
fun deposit(cents: Long) {
    balanceCents += cents      // read, add, write
}

javap shows getfield, ladd and putfield this time: the same three steps for a long field, with the same gaps. The usual next move is to keep the balances in something thread-safe, that is, safe to use from many threads at once. The JDK's ConcurrentHashMap is a map built for exactly that, so let's key the balances by account id and put both ideas through one test.

LostDepositDemo plays out payday. It starts eight teller threads (a teller is the bank clerk who takes your deposit), and each one puts 200,000 one-cent deposits into the same account. It does that three times: with a plain field, with a ConcurrentHashMap and a get plus a put, and with the same map and one call:

Java
balanceCents += 1;                                   // 1. Naive: a plain field
balances.put(ACCOUNT, balances.get(ACCOUNT) + 1);    // 2. Naive: a thread-safe map, two calls
balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::sum);              // 3. Fixed: the same map, one call
Kotlin
balanceCents += 1                                    // 1. Naive: a plain field
balances[ACCOUNT] = balances.getValue(ACCOUNT) + 1   // 2. Naive: a thread-safe map, two calls
balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::plus)              // 3. Fixed: the same map, one call

Before you read the output, guess which of the three come out exact. One run printed:

balanceCents += 1    expected 1,600,000 cents, got 440,684 (lost 1,159,316)
put(get() + 1)       expected 1,600,000 cents, got 329,204 (lost 1,270,796)
merge(1, Long::sum)  expected 1,600,000 cents, got 1,600,000 (lost 0)

The plain field lost more than two thirds of the deposits. With eight threads on four cores, collisions are the normal case.

The second line is the setback, and the one that surprises people. ConcurrentHashMap is a fine tool, and every single call on it is thread-safe. The map kept every promise it makes. It never promised anything about two calls in a row.

put(get() + 1) is two calls, and the gap between them belongs to nobody. Two tellers get the same old balance, both add a cent, and both put the result back.

The third line is the fix. merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::sum) does what the three plain steps do: read the old balance, add the amount, put the result back. But the map runs all three as one atomic step on that key, so no other teller can slip in between. Read it aloud as "add one cent to this balance, whatever it is right now".

A thread-safe class makes each call atomic. Two calls in a row are still a race.

Read-modify-write hides in arithmetic. The second shape of race hides in an if.

try.title: Lose deposits three ways
steps: Read LostDepositDemo (or its Kotlin twin). For each of the three lines it prints, write down whether you expect it to be exact.
Run it with the command below. Then run it twice more and compare the losses.

In version 2, replace the put(get() + 1) line with balances.compute(ACCOUNT, (k, v) -> v + 1) (in Kotlin, balances.compute(ACCOUNT) { _, v -> (v ?: 0L) + 1 }). Predict whether it comes out exact, then run it.

code.title: LostDepositDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Eight teller threads put one-cent deposits into the same bank account, three ways. */ public class LostDepositDemo { static final int THREADS = 8; static final int DEPOSITS = 200_000; // per thread, one cent each static final String ACCOUNT = "account-42"; // volatile only so the JIT re-reads the field every time, as in RaceDemo. It does NOT make += safe. static volatile long balanceCents; static final Map<String, Long> balances = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { balanceCents = 0; runTellers(() -> balanceCents += 1); // 1. a plain field report("balanceCents += 1", balanceCents); balances.put(ACCOUNT, 0L); runTellers(() -> balances.put(ACCOUNT, balances.get(ACCOUNT) + 1)); // 2. a thread-safe map, two calls report("put(get() + 1)", balances.get(ACCOUNT)); balances.put(ACCOUNT, 0L); runTellers(() -> balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::sum)); // 3. the same map, one call report("merge(1, Long::sum)", balances.get(ACCOUNT)); } static void runTellers(Runnable deposit) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] tellers = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int c = 0; c < THREADS; c++) { tellers[c] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < DEPOSITS; i++) deposit.run(); }, "teller-" + c); tellers[c].start(); } for (Thread t : tellers) t.join(); } static void report(String how, long cents) { long expected = (long) THREADS * DEPOSITS; System.out.printf("%-20s expected %,d cents, got %,d (lost %,d)%n", how, expected, cents, expected - cents); } }

alt.title: LostDepositDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight teller threads put one-cent deposits into the same bank account, three ways. private const val TELLERS = 8 private const val DEPOSITS = 200_000 // per thread, one cent each private const val ACCOUNT = "account-42" // @Volatile only so the JIT re-reads the field every time, as in RaceDemo. It does NOT make += safe. @Volatile private var balanceCents = 0L private val balances = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() fun main() { balanceCents = 0 runTellers { balanceCents += 1 } // 1. a plain field report("balanceCents += 1", balanceCents) balances[ACCOUNT] = 0L runTellers { balances[ACCOUNT] = balances.getValue(ACCOUNT) + 1 } // 2. a thread-safe map, two calls report("put(get() + 1)", balances.getValue(ACCOUNT)) balances[ACCOUNT] = 0L runTellers { balances.merge(ACCOUNT, 1L, Long::plus) } // 3. the same map, one call report("merge(1, Long::plus)", balances.getValue(ACCOUNT)) } private fun runTellers(deposit: () -> Unit) { val tellers = List(TELLERS) { c -> thread(name = "teller-$c") { repeat(DEPOSITS) { deposit() } } } tellers.forEach { it.join() } } private fun report(how: String, cents: Long) { val expected = TELLERS.toLong() * DEPOSITS println("%-20s expected %,d cents, got %,d (lost %,d)".format(how, expected, cents, expected - cents)) }

try.expect: The first two lines lose a large share of the 1,600,000 cents, a different amount every run. merge is exact every time. So is compute: like merge, it runs your function inside the map, as one step on that key, so no other teller can change the balance halfway through.

sections.h: Check-then-act: recording the same payment twice
sections.html:
The deposits add up now. The other thing a bank must never do is record the same payment twice.

Copies do arrive. Picture a customer who taps Pay in a phone app on a slow network. The app hears nothing back for a few seconds, so it sends the payment again, to be safe. Now two copies of one payment reach the bank, and two threads can handle them at the same moment. So the bank's program keeps a map of the payments it has recorded, and checks it first:

Java
if (!recordedBy.containsKey(paymentId)) {   // check
    checkPayment(payment);                  // a slow step
    recordedBy.put(paymentId, me);          // act
    record(payment);                        // the money moves
}
Kotlin
if (!recordedBy.containsKey(paymentId)) {   // check
    checkPayment(payment)                   // a slow step
    recordedBy[paymentId] = me              // act
    record(payment)                         // the money moves
}

recordedBy is a ConcurrentHashMap again, and again every call on it is thread-safe. The code still records payments twice. Two tellers can both check, both see "not recorded yet", and both go on to record it. The second put quietly replaces the first teller's name, and the money moves twice.

This shape is check-then-act: you test a condition, then act on it, assuming it still holds. The gap between the check and the act is where the race lives, and the slow step, making sure the payment is genuine, makes that gap wide. The figure shows two tellers inside it at the same time.

DoublePostingDemo (to post a payment is bank talk for recording it) exaggerates on purpose, so the gap is easy to see. Eight tellers all receive the same 1,000 payments, as if every payment arrived eight times. A short spin loop, a loop that only burns time, stands in for the slow check. One run printed:

payments: 1,000  times recorded: 2,579  duplicates: 1,579

Each customer paid once. The shops they paid got 2,579 payments, which made for a very good evening.

The same shape hides in two places you'll meet often. An overdraft check keeps an account from going below zero: if (balanceCents >= cents) balanceCents -= cents;. Yet two withdrawals can both see enough money, and the account goes below zero anyway. Lazy loading, which means creating something only the first time it's needed, if (prices == null) prices = loadPrices();, can load twice.

The fix is one call that does both the check and the act, so no gap is left:

Java
checkPayment(payment);                                // still slow, but no longer inside a gap
if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(paymentId, me) == null) {  // Fixed: check and act in one call
    record(payment);                                  // only one teller gets here
}
Kotlin
checkPayment(payment)                                 // still slow, but no longer inside a gap
if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(paymentId, me) == null) {  // Fixed: the same JDK call from Kotlin
    record(payment)                                   // only one teller gets here
}

Read putIfAbsent as "claim this key, unless someone already has". It returns the previous owner, or null if there was none, and only one caller can ever get that null. Inside, the map does the lookup and the insert as one step on that key's slot, as lesson 9 of this track shows.

computeIfAbsent, merge and Set.add (which returns false if the element was already there) exist for the same reason. Sometimes several copies of the program run on different computers. Then the same idea moves into the database they all share, the program that keeps their data on disk. Make the payment id a unique key, insert it first, and let the second insert fail.

A check is out of date the moment it returns. Make the check and the act one call.

Both fixes so far came from the library: one call that does the whole job on one key. Before we meet a job that needs two keys, let's pin down what any fix has to do.

try.title: Record a payment twice, then once
steps: Run DoublePostingDemo with the command below. Eight tellers race through the same 1,000 payments. Note the duplicates.

Replace the check and the put with one call: if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(payment, me) == null) recorded.incrementAndGet(); (in Kotlin, if (recordedBy.putIfAbsent(payment, "teller-$c") == null) recorded.incrementAndGet()). Keep the spin loop just before it.

code.title: DoublePostingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * The same 1,000 payments reach eight teller threads, as if every payment arrived eight times. * Each teller records a payment only if nobody has recorded it yet: check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. */ public class DoublePostingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<Integer, String> recordedBy = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // payment id -> the teller that recorded it AtomicInteger recorded = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] tellers = new Thread[8]; for (int c = 0; c < tellers.length; c++) { String me = "teller-" + c; tellers[c] = new Thread(() -> { for (int payment = 0; payment < 1_000; payment++) { if (!recordedBy.containsKey(payment)) { // check for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // a slow step: is the payment genuine? recordedBy.put(payment, me); // act recorded.incrementAndGet(); // the money moves } } }, me); } for (Thread t : tellers) t.start(); for (Thread t : tellers) t.join(); System.out.printf("payments: 1,000 times recorded: %,d duplicates: %,d%n", recorded.get(), recorded.get() - 1_000); } }

alt.title: DoublePostingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same 1,000 payments reach eight teller threads, as if every payment arrived eight times. // Each teller records a payment only if nobody has recorded it yet: check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. fun main() { val recordedBy = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, String>() // payment id -> the teller that recorded it val recorded = AtomicInteger() val tellers = List(8) { c -> thread(start = false, name = "teller-$c") { for (payment in 0 until 1_000) { if (!recordedBy.containsKey(payment)) { // check repeat(300) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // a slow step: is the payment genuine? recordedBy[payment] = "teller-$c" // act recorded.incrementAndGet() // the money moves } } } } tellers.forEach { it.start() } tellers.forEach { it.join() } println("payments: 1,000 times recorded: %,d duplicates: %,d".format(recorded.get(), recorded.get() - 1_000)) }

try.expect: The first run records hundreds or thousands of payments more than once (one run here: 2,579 times recorded for 1,000 payments). After the change it records exactly 1,000, every run, with the slow step still inside the loop. Every teller still runs the slow check, but only one of them gets to record each payment.

sections.h: What every fix has to do, and where one call stops
sections.html:
We've met three races and fixed two. Both fixes did the same two jobs, and every fix you write will too.

A fix makes the compound action, the group of steps that must happen together, atomic, so no other thread can run in the middle of it. It also makes the result visible, so the next thread to look sees the new value, not an old copy. Visibility gets its own track later, and every tool below gives you both.

Here are the options, in the order I reach for them.

The first is not to share at all. Give each thread its own counter and add them up after the joins, as the shop's sales total did with its partial array in Threads from zero. Or give every account to exactly one thread, so no other thread ever touches its balance. No sharing, no race.

The second is one atomic call that the library already has: merge, putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, Set.add, or an atomic class such as AtomicLong, a number whose updates happen in one step. These calls are fast and hard to get wrong, and lesson 8 of this track opens them up.

The third is a lock around the whole compound action. A lock lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, and the others wait at the door until it's free. Mark a method synchronized, and Java puts a lock around it. A lock works for any code, even a change to two balances at once. The price is that every caller waits in line.

A lock comes with two conditions. It must cover the reads: a synchronized setter with a plain getter is still broken, because nothing promises the reader the latest value. And it must cover the whole action, since locking containsKey and put separately leaves the same gap between them.

Every access to shared state goes through the same lock or the same atomic. Guard the reads too.

For the counter, each fix is one line, and the Try it below has you make both. In five runs each on a 4-core machine, both printed 2,000,000 every time. The AtomicInteger version took 41 to 54 ms a run, close to the broken one.

The synchronized version took anywhere from 28 to 220 ms. The JIT compiler and the scheduler decide how long each thread keeps the lock before the other gets a turn, and that changes from run to run. So correctness is settled, and speed is something to measure more than once.

That brings us to the limit of today's tools. Every fix so far protects one thing: one counter, one key, one balance. A transfer takes money out of one account and puts it into another. No one may see the money in flight, gone from the first account and not yet in the second.

No single map call moves money between two keys, and two atomic calls in a row are just a new gap. That job needs a lock, and a lock has rules of its own.

try.title: Fix RaceDemo two ways
steps: In RaceDemo, add static synchronized void inc() { count++; } and call inc() in the loop. (In Kotlin, add a top-level private val lock = Any() and write synchronized(lock) { count++ } in the loop.) Run it.

Undo that. Change count to static final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(); (in Kotlin, private val count = AtomicInteger()), call count.incrementAndGet(), reset it with count.set(0) and print count.get(). Run it.
Which one felt slower? Add long t0 = System.nanoTime(); before the threads start, print the elapsed milliseconds after the joins, and run each version a few times.
try.expect: Both versions print exactly 2,000,000 on all five runs. The times jump around. On a 4-core Linux machine the atomic version took 41 to 54 ms a run, close to the broken one, and the synchronized one took anywhere from 28 to 220 ms. Get it correct first, then measure the speed, and measure more than once.

compare.title: The same race and fix in Java and Kotlin

java.title: AccountBalance.java
java.html: public class AccountBalance { private long balanceCents; // Naive: balanceCents += cents is a read, an add and a write public void depositBroken(long cents) { balanceCents += cents; } // Fixed: one thread at a time, and readers take the same lock public synchronized void deposit(long cents) { balanceCents += cents; } public synchronized long balance() { return balanceCents; } }

kotlin.title: AccountBalance.kt
kotlin.html: class AccountBalance { private var balanceCents = 0L // Naive: compiles to the same read, add and write fun depositBroken(cents: Long) { balanceCents += cents } // Fixed: Kotlin has no synchronized modifier; the annotation does the same job @Synchronized fun deposit(cents: Long) { balanceCents += cents } @Synchronized fun balance(): Long = balanceCents }

compare.note: Both classes have the same race and the same fix, and the Kotlin one is a direct translation. Two things differ. Kotlin has no synchronized modifier, so the fix is the @Synchronized annotation, which marks the compiled method as synchronized exactly as Java's modifier does. And += on a Kotlin var property compiles to the same read, add and write as Java's, so it races in exactly the same way. java.util.concurrent.atomic and ConcurrentHashMap.merge work the same from both languages.

worked.title: Find and fix the race in the bank's duplicate check

steps.say: The bank's payment desk skips payments it has already recorded, so that a copy sent twice by the phone app is ignored. It runs on four threads, and recording a payment takes about 80 ms. ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() gives a thread-safe set. Read the code and find the shape before you read on.
steps.code: class PaymentDesk { private final Set<String> recorded = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); void handle(Payment p) { if (recorded.contains(p.id())) return; // check bank.record(p); // about 80 ms recorded.add(p.id()); // act } }

alt.html: class PaymentDesk { private val recorded: MutableSet<String> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() fun handle(p: Payment) { if (p.id in recorded) return // check bank.record(p) // about 80 ms recorded += p.id // act } }

steps.say: It's check-then-act, with an 80 ms gap. Two copies of the same payment, handled by two threads within the same 80 ms, both pass the contains check, and both get recorded. The set being thread-safe doesn't help, because the race is between the calls, not inside them.

Claim the id first, in one atomic call. Set.add returns false if the id was already there, so only one thread gets past the first line. If recording fails, release the claim, so that a retry can have another go.
steps.code: void handle(Payment p) { // 1. claim the id: add() returns false if it was already there if (!recorded.add(p.id())) return; try { bank.record(p); // 2. record } catch (RuntimeException ex) { recorded.remove(p.id()); // 3. release on failure throw ex; } }

alt.html: fun handle(p: Payment) { // 1. claim the id: add() returns false if it was already there if (!recorded.add(p.id)) return try { bank.record(p) // 2. record } catch (ex: RuntimeException) { recorded.remove(p.id) // 3. release on failure throw ex } }

steps.say: That closes the race inside one running program. It doesn't survive a restart, and it doesn't cover a second copy of the program running on another computer. For those, the claim belongs in the database that every copy shares, the program that keeps the bank's data on disk. Insert the payment id into a table where ids must be unique, before recording, and treat a duplicate-key error as "already recorded". It's the same idea, one atomic step, moved to the place that every copy can see.
steps.code: INSERT INTO recorded_payment (payment_id, received_at) VALUES (?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP); -- a second insert with the same id fails

lab.title: Make threads collide, then fix two races
steps: Meet the three classes. Hammer is a helper you'll write: it starts several threads and releases them at the same moment, so they really collide. HitCounter counts visits to a web page, and each visit calls hit() from its own thread. SeatMap sells the seats of a small concert hall, and each seat may be sold only once.

Run the tests once. All five should fail. Read the messages: Hammer isn't written yet, the counter comes up short, and seats are sold more than once. (The counter test runs five rounds, because one round on broken code can get lucky: the threads don't always collide, just as in the first section.)

Write Hammer.run with two CountDownLatch objects. A CountDownLatch is a gate that opens when its count reaches zero: countDown() lowers the count, and await() waits for the gate to open. Create a latch ready of size threads and a latch go of size 1. Each thread calls ready.countDown(), waits on go.await(), then runs the task. The caller waits on ready, calls go.countDown(), then joins every thread.
Fix HitCounter so 8 threads x 200,000 hits always add up. Guard the read too.
Fix SeatMap.book without synchronized. It's the recorded-payments check from this lesson, with concert seats in it: replace the check and the put with one map call. Keep the call to priceTheSeat().
Run the tests again until all five pass. Then run them three more times. A race fix has to pass every time, not most of the time.
hints: Why two latches in Hammer? ready tells the caller that every thread exists and is waiting. go releases them all at the same instant. Without ready, the first threads could finish before the last ones are even created.
Inside a thread's lambda, go.await() throws InterruptedException. Catch it, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(), and return, as in A thread's life.
putIfAbsent returns the previous value, or null if there was none. Only one caller can ever get null for a given key.
lab.done: All five tests in RaceConditionsTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the start-line harness from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. In a blank file, write static void collide(int n, Runnable task): it starts n threads, releases them at the same moment, and returns when all of them are done. Then compare with the answer. Did you remember the join?

answer.html: static void collide(int n, Runnable task) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(n); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } task.run(); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } ready.await(); // all waiting at the start line go.countDown(); // starting gun for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); }

alt.html: fun collide(n: Int, task: () -> Unit) { val ready = CountDownLatch(n) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(n) { thread { ready.countDown() try { go.await() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return@thread } task() } } ready.await() // all waiting at the start line go.countDown() // starting gun threads.forEach { it.join() } }

recap: A race condition is a bug where the result depends on how threads take turns. It gives wrong answers quietly, and small tests hide it, so make threads collide on purpose.
count++, balanceCents += cents and put(k, get(k) + x) are read-modify-write: when two threads read the same old value, one update is lost.
Check-then-act (if (!containsKey) put, if (x == null) x = ...) breaks when another thread acts in the gap between the check and the act.
A thread-safe collection makes each call atomic, never a sequence of calls. Use the one call that does the whole job: merge, putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent or Set.add.
Fixes, in order of preference: don't share, use one atomic library call, or lock the whole compound action, reads included.
The limit: one atomic call protects one variable or one key. A change that spans two, like a transfer between accounts, needs a lock.

explain.prompt: A friend says: "Our recorded-payments map is a ConcurrentHashMap, so the program can't record a payment twice." Explain to them, in your own words, why that is wrong and what you would change.
explain.answer: ConcurrentHashMap makes each single call atomic, so containsKey and put are each safe on their own. The program runs them as two separate steps: check whether the payment was recorded, then mark it recorded. Another thread can run the same check between those two calls, so two threads both see the payment as new and both record it. The fix is to do the check and the act in one call, putIfAbsent(paymentId, me) == null, so only one thread can ever win. If several copies of the program run on different computers, the same idea moves into their shared database as a unique key.

deeper.html:
Two terms sound alike and mean different things.

A data race is a precise term from the Java Language Specification (JLS), the official rulebook of the language, in chapter 17. Two threads access the same variable, at least one of the accesses is a write, and nothing orders the two accesses by a happens-before relationship, an ordering guarantee such as the one join() gives. A program with a data race can see surprising values, because the compiler and the CPU are allowed to reorder and cache unsynchronized accesses.

A race condition is a logic bug: the program is wrong under some interleavings, some orders in which the threads' steps can mix. You can have either one without the other. The fixed payment desk from the worked example has no data race, since every access goes through the thread-safe set. But between the claim and the release on failure, other threads can see a payment that is recorded and then unrecorded again. That's a race condition built entirely from thread-safe calls. Going the other way, String.hashCode() caches its result in a plain field that several threads may write at once. That's a data race, but a harmless one: every thread computes the same value, and an int write can't tear, that is, can't be seen half written.

long and double are the exception to that last point. JLS section 17.7 allows a write to a non-volatile long or double to happen as two separate 32-bit writes, so another thread could read half of an old value and half of a new one. 64-bit JVMs write them in one go in practice, but the specification only promises it when the field is volatile.

You'll meet happens-before properly in the memory model track. Until then, the rule from the last section holds: every access to shared mutable state, reads included, goes through the same lock or the same atomic variable.
